planting.note: Plant seed-yam setts (small whole tubers or sett pieces with intact skin) on mounds or ridges 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed well past last frost; stake or trellis vines early since they climb vigorously.

directions: Obiaoturugo is a long-cultivated white yam landrace grown across southeastern Nigeria, prized by Igbo farmers and households for the smooth, elastic texture it gives pounded yam (iyan) once boiled and mashed. Vines are trained up stakes or a trellis from mounds or ridges of loose, well-drained soil, and tubers are left to bulk for 8 to 10 months before the foliage yellows and dies back at harvest. The cultivar remains an important reference landrace in Nigerian yam breeding and agronomy trials alongside improved hybrids, valued for culinary quality even where raw yield lags behind newer selections. As with other yam landraces central to Igbo culture, tubers from this variety are traditionally tied to the New Yam Festival (Iri Ji) that marks the harvest season.
sources: National Root Crops Research Institute (NRCRI), Umudike, Nigeria

common_name: Alumaco Yam (Nigerian High-Yielding White Yam Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant whole small seed tubers or minisetts on ridges or mounds of loose, fertile soil once danger of frost has passed, and train the twining vines up stakes as they emerge.

directions: Alumaco is a white yam cultivar from Nigeria's yam belt that has repeatedly out-yielded other local landraces and some improved lines in agronomic comparison trials, producing a higher number of seed-yam and ware-yam tubers per plot along with a faster bulking rate. Farmers propagate it from whole small tubers or minisetts planted on ridges or mounds of loose, fertile soil, training the twining vines up stakes as they emerge. Because of its productivity, Alumaco is frequently included in on-farm trials evaluating seed-yam multiplication techniques within Nigeria's Guinea yam system. Tubers mature over roughly 8 to 10 months and are harvested once vines senesce and skins toughen enough for storage.
sources: National Root Crops Research Institute (NRCRI), Umudike, Nigeria

common_name: Afisiafi Cassava (Ghana's Most Widely Adopted Improved Variety)

planting.note: Plant 8-10 inch stem cuttings (stakes) horizontally or at a 45-degree angle, 2-4 inches deep, once soil has warmed well past 65°F; Afisiafi stakes root readily and establish quickly compared to many older Ghanaian landraces.

directions: Released in 1993 by Ghana's CSIR-Crops Research Institute, Afisiafi was one of three high-yielding, disease-tolerant cassava varieties launched that year and quickly became the most widely adopted improved cassava variety among Ghanaian farmers. Root yields of 28 to 35 tonnes per hectare, well above many local landraces, combined with solid tolerance to cassava mosaic disease, drove its rapid uptake across Ghana's cassava belt. The roots carry roughly 32 percent dry matter, a profile well suited to gari, cassava flour, and starch processing as well as direct boiling. As with other cassava, stakes are planted horizontally in well-drained soil and the crop is left to bulk for 12 to 15 months before harvest.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) — Cassava in Africa country case studies

planting.note: Plant disease-free stem cuttings horizontally 2-4 inches deep in well-drained soil once soil has warmed past 65°F; space generously since this variety grows a full, productive canopy.

directions: Bankyehemaa — a Twi name combining bankye ("cassava") and hemaa ("queen") — was released in 2005 by Ghana's CSIR-Crops Research Institute alongside two sister varieties, Essam Bankye and Dokuduade, all bred for tolerance to cassava mosaic disease. It matures in about 9 to 12 months and produces exceptionally high root yields of 40 to 50 tonnes per hectare with roughly 32 percent dry matter, making it popular among Ghanaian farmers seeking both productivity and good processing quality for flour, gari, and fufu. Propagate from healthy stem cuttings planted horizontally in well-drained soil in full sun; the plant tolerates poor soils and periodic drought once established, though yields improve substantially with moderate fertility and consistent moisture during early establishment.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) — Cassava in Africa country case studies

planting.note: Plant seed potato pieces (2-3 eyes each) in cool, loose, fertile soil; Pastusa Suprema was bred for the cool, high-altitude growing conditions of Colombia's Nariño department and performs best with cool days and nights similar to its native highland climate.

directions: Released in 2002 as an improved successor to the older Pastusa Parda landrace, Pastusa Suprema takes its name from Pasto, capital of Colombia's high-Andean Nariño department, where it was developed for the region's cool, high-elevation growing conditions. It combines resistance to late blight with high tuber solids and low oil absorption when fried, qualities that made it Colombia's leading commercial potato variety by 2009, used for both fresh table consumption and processing into chips and fries. The tubers are larger than the yellow-fleshed Criolla-type potatoes also grown in Colombia, with a drier, mealier character suited to frying and roasting rather than the waxy texture of diploid Criolla types. Grow as a standard potato: plant seed pieces in loose, fertile, well-drained soil, hill as plants grow, and harvest once vines die back; the variety performs best with cool growing temperatures and a season long enough to bulk tubers before summer heat arrives.
sources: Corporación Colombiana de Investigación Agropecuaria (Agrosavia, formerly Corpoica)
